Tajikistan
Tajikistan, officially the Republic of Tajikistan, is a landlocked country located in <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>. <color=#3366CC>Dushanbe</color> is the <color=#3366CC>capital</color>
and largest city of the country, with a population of over 1.2 million. Tajikistan borders <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color> to the south,

<color=#3366CC>Uzbekistan</color> to the west, <color=#3366CC>Kyrgyzstan</color> to the north, and <color=#3366CC>China</color> to the east; it is narrowly separated from <color=#3366CC>Pakistan</color> by
Afghanistan's <color=#3366CC>Wakhan Corridor</color>. Its total population exceeds 11 million.
The territory was previously home to cultures of the <color=#3366CC>Neolithic</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Bronze Age</color>, including the <color=#3366CC>Oxus civilisation</color> in the
west. Parts of the country were part of the <color=#3366CC>Sogdian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bactrian</color> civilisations, and were ruled by the <color=#3366CC>Achaemenids</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color>, the <color=#3366CC>GrecoBactrians</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Kushans</color>, the Kidarites, the Hephthalites, the <color=#3366CC>First Turkic Khaganate</color>, the

<color=#3366CC>Umayyad</color> and <color=#3366CC>Abbasid Caliphates</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Samanid Empire</color>, the <color=#3366CC>KaraKhanids</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Seljuks</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Khwarazmians</color>, the

<color=#3366CC>Mongols</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Timurids</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Khanate of Bukhara</color>. The region was <color=#3366CC>later conquered</color> by the <color=#3366CC>Russian Empire</color>, before
becoming part of the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>. Within the Soviet Union, the country's borders were drawn when it was part of
Uzbekistan as an autonomous republic, before becoming a constituent republic of the Soviet Union on 5 December
On 9 September 1991, Tajikistan declared itself an independent sovereign state as <color=#3366CC>the Soviet Union was disintegrating</color>.
A <color=#3366CC>civil war</color> was fought after independence, lasting from May 1992 to June 1997. Since the end of the war, newly
established political stability and foreign aid have allowed the country's economy to grow. The country has been led
since 1994 by <color=#3366CC>Emomali Rahmon</color>, who heads an <color=#3366CC>authoritarian regime</color> and whose human rights record has been
criticised.
Tajikistan is a <color=#3366CC>presidential republic</color> consisting of four provinces. Tajiks form the ethnic majority in the country, and their
national language is <color=#3366CC>Tajik</color>. <color=#3366CC>Russian</color> is used as the official interethnic language. While the state is constitutionally
secular, Islam is adhered to by 97.5% of the population. In the Gorno-Badakhshan oblast, there is considerable
linguistic diversity, with languages such as Rushani, Shughni, Ishkashimi, Wakhi, and Tajik being spoken. Mountains
cover more than 90% of the country. It is a <color=#3366CC>developing country</color> with a transitional economy that is dependent on

remittances and on the production of <color=#3366CC>aluminium</color> and <color=#3366CC>cotton</color>. Tajikistan is a member of the <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color>, <color=#3366CC>CIS</color>, <color=#3366CC>OSCE</color>,
<color=#3366CC>OIC</color>, <color=#3366CC>ECO</color>, <color=#3366CC>SCO</color>, and <color=#3366CC>CSTO</color>, and is a <color=#3366CC>NATO</color> PfP partner.
Etymology
The term 'Tajik' ultimately derives from the Middle Persian Tāzīk, the <color=#3366CC>Turkic</color> rendition of the <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color> ethnonym Tayyi’,
denoting a Qahtanite Arab tribe that migrated to the Transoxiana region of <color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color> in the 7th century AD. Before
1991, Tajikistan appeared in English as Tadjikistan or Tadzhikistan. This is owing to a transliteration from the. In
Russian, there is no single letter 'j' to represent the phoneme; instead, (transliterated as dzh) is used. Tadzhikistan is an
alternative spelling and is found in Englishlanguage literature derived from Russian sources.
History
Cultures in the region have been dated back to at least the fourth millennium BC, including the <color=#3366CC>Bronze Age</color>
<color=#3366CC>Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Andronovo culture</color> and the pro-urban site of Sarazm, a UNESCO <color=#3366CC>World</color>
<color=#3366CC>Heritage Site</color>.
The earliest recorded history of the region dates back to about 500 BC when most, if not all, of Tajikistan was a part of
the <color=#3366CC>Achaemenid Empire</color>. Some authors have suggested that in the seventh and sixth centuries BC parts of Tajikistan,
including territories in the Zeravshan Valley, formed part of the Kambojas before they became part of the Achaemenid
Empire. After the region's conquest by <color=#3366CC>Alexander the Great</color> it became part of the <color=#3366CC>Greco-Bactrian Kingdom</color>, a successor
state of Alexander's empire. Northern Tajikistan (the cities of <color=#3366CC>Khujand</color> and Panjakent) was a part of <color=#3366CC>Sogdiana</color>, a
collection of city-states which were overrun by Scytho-Siberians and <color=#3366CC>Yuezhi</color> nomadic tribes around 150 BC. The <color=#3366CC>Silk</color>
<color=#3366CC>Road</color> passed through the region and following the expedition of Chinese explorer <color=#3366CC>Zhang Qian</color> during the reign of <color=#3366CC>Wudi</color>
(141 BC – 87 BC) commercial relations between <color=#3366CC>Han Empire</color> and Sogdiana flourished. Sogdians played a role in
facilitating trade and worked in other capacities, as farmers, carpetweavers, glassmakers, and woodcarvers.
The <color=#3366CC>Kushan Empire</color>, a collection of Yuezhi tribes, took control of the region in the first century AD and ruled until the
fourth century AD during which time <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>, Nestorian Christianity, <color=#3366CC>Zoroastrianism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Manichaeism</color> were
practised in the region. Later the Hephthalite Empire, a collection of nomadic tribes, moved into the region, and the
<color=#3366CC>Arabs</color> propagated Islam in the eighth century.
Samanid Empire
Four brothers – Nuh, Ahmad, Yahya, and Ilyas – founded the <color=#3366CC>Samanid Empire</color>. Each of them ruled territory under
<color=#3366CC>Abbasid</color> suzerainty. In 892, <color=#3366CC>Ismail Samani</color> (892–907) united the Samanid state under a single ruler, thereby putting an
end to the feudal system that had previously prevailed. It was under his rule that the Samanids became independent of
Abbasid authority. The Samanid Empire (819–999) restored <color=#3366CC>Persian</color> control of the region and expanded the cities of

<color=#3366CC>Samarkand</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bukhara</color>, which became the cultural centres of the <color=#3366CC>Iranian world</color>; the region was known as <color=#3366CC>Khorasan</color>.
The empire was centred on Khorasan and Transoxiana, and at its greatest extent encompassed Afghanistan, parts of
Iran, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, parts of Kazakhstan, and Pakistan.
The Samanids revived <color=#3366CC>Persian culture</color> by patronising <color=#3366CC>Rudaki</color>, Bal'ami, and Daqiqi. The Samanids actively promoted
Sunni Islam and suppressed <color=#3366CC>Ismaili</color> Shi'ism, but were more tolerant of <color=#3366CC>Twelver</color> Shi'ism. Islamic architecture and
PersoIslamic culture were spread deep into the heartlands of Central Asia by the Samanids. Following the first
complete translation of the Qur'an into Persian in the 9th century, populations under the Samanid Empire began to
accept Islam in significant numbers.
The Karluk Turkic <color=#3366CC>Kara-Khanid Khanate</color> conquered Transoxania (which corresponded approximately to what would
later become Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, southern Kyrgyzstan, and southwest Kazakhstan) and ruled there from 999 to
1211. Their arrival in Transoxania marked a definitive shift from Iranian to Turkic predominance in Central Asia. Over
time, the KaraKhanids became assimilated into the PersoArab Muslim culture of the region.
The region was later ruled by the <color=#3366CC>Ghurid</color> and Kart dynasties, both of Tajik origin. While the Kart dynasty ruled in
presentday Afghanistan, <color=#3366CC>Muhammad of Ghor</color>, a ruler of the Ghurid dynasty, conquered large parts of India.
In the 13th century, the <color=#3366CC>Mongol Empire</color> swept through Central Asia, invaded the <color=#3366CC>Khwarezmian Empire</color>, and sacked its
cities, looting and massacring their inhabitants. The TurcoMongol conqueror <color=#3366CC>Tamerlane</color> founded the <color=#3366CC>Timurid Empire</color>,
becoming the first ruler of the Timurid dynasty in what later became Tajikistan and Central Asia.
Bukharan rule
The territory that later became Tajikistan came under the rule of the <color=#3366CC>Khanate of Bukhara</color> during the 16th century.
Following the khanate's collapse in the 18th century, the region fell under the control of the <color=#3366CC>Emirate of Bukhara</color> and the
<color=#3366CC>Khanate of Kokand</color>. The Emirate of Bukhara remained intact until the 20th century.
Imperial Russia
During the 19th century, the Russian Empire began to conquer parts of the region. Russian <color=#3366CC>Imperialism</color> led to the
<color=#3366CC>Russian Empire</color>'s conquest of Central Asia during the 19th century's <color=#3366CC>Imperial Era</color>. Between 1864 and 1885, Russia
gradually took control of the entire territory of Russian Turkestan, the Tajikistan portion of which had been controlled by
the Emirate of Bukhara and Khanate of Kokand. Russia was interested in gaining access to a supply of <color=#3366CC>cotton</color> and in
the 1870s attempted to switch cultivation in the region from grain to cotton (a strategy later copied and expanded by the
Soviets).
During the 19th century, the Jadidists established themselves as an Islamic social movement throughout the region.
While the Jadidists were pro-modernisation and not necessarily anti-Russian, the Russians viewed the movement as a
threat because the Russian Empire was predominantly Christian. Russian troops were required to restore order during
uprisings against the Khanate of Kokand between 1910 and 1913. Further violence occurred in July 1916 when
demonstrators attacked Russian soldiers in Khujand over the threat of forced <color=#3366CC>conscription</color> during <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>. While
Russian troops brought Khujand back under control, clashes continued throughout the year in various locations in
Tajikistan.
Soviet period
After the <color=#3366CC>Russian Revolution</color> of 1917, guerrillas throughout Central Asia, known as basmachi, waged a war against
<color=#3366CC>Bolshevik</color> armies in an attempt to maintain independence. The Bolsheviks prevailed after a fouryear war, during which
<color=#3366CC>mosques</color> and villages were burned down and the population was suppressed.
Between 1928 and 1941, Soviet authorities began an antireligious campaign of <color=#3366CC>secularisation</color>. Practising <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, or <color=#3366CC>Judaism</color> was discouraged and repressed; under Soviet anti-religious legislation, several <color=#3366CC>churches</color>, <color=#3366CC>mosques</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>synagogues</color> were closed. As a consequence of the conflict and Soviet agricultural policies, Central Asia, including
Tajikistan, suffered a famine that claimed many lives.
Tajikistan was first created in 1924 as the Tajik Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic (abbreviated as the Tajik ASSR),
an autonomous republic within the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic. Despite their historical status as Tajik cities and
their largely Tajik populations, none of the regional urban centres – such as <color=#3366CC>Bukhara</color>, <color=#3366CC>Samarkand</color>, Tirmiz, <color=#3366CC>Qarshi</color>, and
Khojand – were included in Tajikistan. Instead, the Tajikistani capital was established in <color=#3366CC>Dushanbe</color>, a mountain town
with approximately 1,000 residents.
A specific Persian dialect, with vocabulary and pronunciation distinct from formal written Persian, was deliberately
made the national language of Tajikistan by the Soviets and renamed 'Tajiki' in order to forcibly separate it from the
common variant of Persian spoken from <color=#3366CC>Istanbul</color> to <color=#3366CC>Calcutta</color>. The Tajiks were also excluded from the enormous global
world of Persian literature, both past and present, by the creation of a new phonetic alphabet – first Latinbased in 1928
and later Cyrillic in 1940. With Persian confined to Tajikistan and replaced by Russian as Central Asia's common
language, the unity of the Persianate world was broken, steering Soviet and postSoviet Central Asia on to a
developmental path distinct from that of Iran and Afghanistan. In 1929, the Tajik ASSR was elevated to its own full
union republic, the Tajik Soviet Socialist Republic. The Sughd Region was added to Tajikistan in the same year.
Between 1927 and 1934, <color=#3366CC>collectivisation of agriculture</color> and an expansion of cotton production took place, especially in
the southern region. Soviet collectivization policy brought violence against farmers and peasants, classified as
anti-Soviet categories of "enemies of the people", and <color=#3366CC>forced resettlement</color> occurred throughout Tajikistan.
Consequently, some peasants fought collectivisation and revived the Basmachi movement. Some industrial
development occurred during this time along with the expansion of irrigation infrastructure.
Two rounds of <color=#3366CC>Stalin's purges</color> (1927–1934 and 1937–1938) resulted in the expulsion of nearly 10,000 people from all
levels of the Communist Party of Tajikistan. Ethnic Russians were sent in to replace those expelled and subsequently
Russians dominated party positions at all levels, including the top position of first secretary. Between 1926 and 1959
the proportion of Russians among Tajikistan's population grew from less than 1% to 13%. Bobojon Ghafurov, First
Secretary of the Communist Party of Tajikistan from 1946 to 1956, was the only Tajik politician of significance outside
of the republic during the Soviet Era.
Tajiks began to be conscripted into the <color=#3366CC>Red Army</color> in 1939, and during the <color=#3366CC>Second World War</color> around 260,000 Tajik
citizens fought against <color=#3366CC>Nazi Germany</color>, Finland, and the <color=#3366CC>Empire of Japan</color>. Between 60,000 (4%) and 120,000 (8%) of
Tajikistan's 1,530,000 citizens were killed during the war.
Following the war and the end of Stalin's rule, attempts were made to further expand the agriculture and industry of
Tajikistan. During 1957–58, <color=#3366CC>Nikita Khrushchev</color>'s Virgin Lands Campaign focused attention on Tajikistan, where living
conditions, education, and industry lagged behind those of the other Soviet republics. In the 1980s, Tajikistan had the
lowest household saving rate in the USSR, the lowest percentage of households in the two top per capita income
groups, and the lowest rate of university graduates per 1,000 people.
By the 1980s, Tajik nationalists were calling for increased rights. Real disturbances did not occur within the republic
until 1990. The following year, the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color> collapsed, and Tajikistan declared its independence on 9 September
1991, a day which is celebrated as the country's Independence Day.
Independence
In February 1990, riots and strikes in Dushanbe and other cities began because of the difficult socioeconomic situation,
a shortage of housing, and youth unemployment. The nationalist and democratic opposition, along with supporters of
independence, joined the strikes and began to demand the independence of the republic and democratic reforms.
<color=#3366CC>Islamists</color> also began to hold strikes to demand respect for their rights and independence. The Soviet leadership
introduced Internal Troops in Dushanbe to put an end to the unrest.
Following independence, the nation fell into <color=#3366CC>civil war</color> among factions distinguished by clan loyalties. Regional groups
from the Gharm and Gorno-Badakhshan regions of Tajikistan, led by a combination of <color=#3366CC>liberal democratic</color> reformers and
<color=#3366CC>Islamists</color>, who eventually became the United Tajik Opposition, rose up against the newly formed government of
President Rahmon Nabiyev, which was dominated by people from the Khujand and Kulob regions.
The war lasted until 1997. More than 500,000 residents fled during this time because of persecution and increased
poverty, seeking better economic opportunities in the West or in other former Soviet republics. The estimated number
of dead exceeded 100,000. Around 1.2 million people were <color=#3366CC>refugees</color>, both inside and outside the country.
<color=#3366CC>Emomali Rahmon</color> came to power in the early part of this conflict in 1992, after Nabiyev was forced at gunpoint on 7
September 1992 to resign from office. Rahmon defeated the former prime minister Abdumalik Abdullajanov in a
presidential election in November with 58% of the vote.
In 1997, a <color=#3366CC>ceasefire</color> was reached between Rahmon and opposition parties under the guidance of Gerd D. Merrem,
Special Representative to the Secretary General, a result praised as a successful United Nations peacekeeping
initiative. The ceasefire guaranteed 30% of ministerial positions would go to the opposition. Elections were held in 1999
and were criticised by opposition parties and foreign observers as unfair; Rahmon was re-elected with 98% of the vote.
Elections in 2006 were again won by Rahmon (with 79% of the vote) and he began his third term in office. Opposition
parties boycotted the 2006 election and the <color=#3366CC>Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe</color> (OSCE) criticised it,
while observers from the <color=#3366CC>Commonwealth of Independent States</color> claimed the elections were legal and transparent.
Rahmon's administration came under further criticism from OSCE in October 2010 for its censorship and repression of
the media. OSCE claimed that the Tajik Government censored Tajik and foreign websites and instituted tax inspections
on independent printing houses that led to the cessation of printing activities for a number of independent newspapers.
Russian border troops were stationed along the Tajik–Afghan border until summer 2005. Since the <color=#3366CC>September 11,</color>
<color=#3366CC>2001 attacks</color>, French troops have been stationed at Dushanbe Airport in support of air operations of <color=#3366CC>NATO</color>'s
International Security Assistance Force in Afghanistan. United States Army and <color=#3366CC>Marine Corps</color> personnel periodically
visit Tajikistan to conduct joint training missions of up to several weeks' duration. The <color=#3366CC>Government of India</color> rebuilt the
Ayni Air Base, a military airport located 15 km southwest of Dushanbe, at a cost of $70 million, completing the repairs
in September 2010. It is the main base of the Tajikistan Air Force. There have been talks with Russia concerning use of
the Ayni facility, and Russia continues to maintain a base on the outskirts of Dushanbe.
In 2010, there were concerns among Tajik officials that Islamic militarism in the east of the country was on the rise
following the escape of 25 militants from a Tajik prison in August, an ambush that killed 28 Tajik soldiers in the Rasht
Valley in September, and another ambush in the valley in October that killed 30 soldiers, followed by fighting outside
Gharm that left three militants dead. The country's Interior Ministry insisted that the central government maintained full
control over the country's east, and the military operation in the Rasht Valley was concluded in November 2010.
Fighting erupted again, this time in and around Gorno-Badakhshan, in July 2012. In 2015, Russia sent more troops to
Tajikistan.
In May 2015, Tajikistan's national security underwent a setback when Colonel Gulmurod Khalimov, commander of the
special-purpose police unit (OMON) of the Interior Ministry, defected to the <color=#3366CC>Islamic State</color>. Khalimov was allegedly killed
on 8 September 2017 during a Russian airstrike near <color=#3366CC>Deir ez-Zor</color>, <color=#3366CC>Syria</color>, although Tajikistan authorities express doubts
whether he has died.
In 2021, following the <color=#3366CC>Fall of Kabul</color>, Tajikistan allegedly got involved in the Panjshir conflict against the <color=#3366CC>Taliban</color> on the
side of the National Resistance Front of Afghanistan.
In September 2022 armed clashes, including the use of artillery, erupted along most of the border between Kyrgyzstan
and Tajikistan.
Geography
Tajikistan is landlocked and is the smallest nation in Central Asia by area. It lies mostly between latitudes 36° and 41°
N, and longitudes 67° and 75° E. It is covered by mountains of the <color=#3366CC>Pamir</color> range, and most of the country is over 3000 m
above <color=#3366CC>sea level</color>. The areas of lower land are in the north (part of the <color=#3366CC>Fergana Valley</color>) and in the southern valleys of the
Kofarnihon and Vakhsh rivers, which form the Amu Darya. <color=#3366CC>Dushanbe</color> is located on the southern slopes above the
Kofarnihon valley.
The <color=#3366CC>Amu Darya</color> and Panj rivers mark the border with Afghanistan, and the glaciers in Tajikistan's mountains are the
source of runoff for the <color=#3366CC>Aral Sea</color>. There are over 900 rivers in Tajikistan longer than 10 kilometres.
Biodiversity
Tajikistan contains five terrestrial ecoregions: Alai-Western Tian Shan steppe, Gissaro-Alai open woodlands, Pamir
alpine desert and tundra, Badghyz and Karabil semi-desert, and Paropamisus xeric woodlands.
Government and politics
After independence, Tajikistan was plunged into a civil war. Factions were supported by foreign countries including
<color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>, Iran, Pakistan, <color=#3366CC>Uzbekistan</color> and Russia. Russia and Iran focused on keeping peace in the warring nation to
decrease the chances of <color=#3366CC>U.S.</color> or <color=#3366CC>Turkish</color> involvement. Russia backed the pro-government faction and deployed troops
from the <color=#3366CC>Commonwealth of Independent States</color> to guard the Tajikistan-Afghan border. All but 25,000 of the more than
400,000 ethnic Russians, who were mostly employed in industry, fled to Russia. By 1997, the war had ended after a
<color=#3366CC>peace agreement</color> between the government and the Islamist-led opposition, and a central government began to take
form, with peaceful elections in 1999.
"Longtime observers of Tajikistan often characterize the country as profoundly averse to risk and skeptical of promises
of reform, a political passivity they trace to the country's ruinous civil war," Ilan Greenberg wrote in a news article in <color=#3366CC>The</color>
<color=#3366CC>New York Times</color> before the country's November 2006 presidential election.
The parliamentary elections of 2005 aroused accusations from opposition parties and international observers that
President <color=#3366CC>Emomali Rahmon</color> corruptly manipulated the election process and unemployment. Elections in February 2010
saw the ruling PDPT lose four seats in Parliament, yet still maintain a majority. The <color=#3366CC>Organization for Security and</color>
<color=#3366CC>Co-operation in Europe</color> election observers said the 2010 polling "failed to meet many key OSCE commitments" and
that "these elections failed on many basic democratic standards." The government insisted that only minor violations
had occurred, which would not affect the will of the Tajik people.
The Tajik government has reportedly clamped down on facial hair as part of a crackdown on Islamic influence and due
to its perceived associations with Islamic extremism, which is evident in bordering <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>.
The presidential election held on 6 November 2006 was boycotted by "mainline" opposition parties, including the
23,000-member Islamic Renaissance Party. Four remaining opponents "all but endorsed the incumbent", Rahmon.
Freedom of the press is officially guaranteed by the government, and independent press outlets remain restricted, as
does an amount of web content. According to the Institute for War & Peace Reporting, access to local and foreign
websites is blocked, and journalists are sometimes obstructed from reporting on some events. In practice, no public
criticism of the regime is tolerated and all direct protest is suppressed and denied coverage in the local media.
In the 2020 Democracy Index by the Economist Intelligence Unit, Tajikistan was ranked 160th, after <color=#3366CC>Saudi Arabia</color>, while
receiving the designation of "authoritarian regime".
In July 2019, UN ambassadors of 37 countries, including Tajikistan, signed a joint letter to UNHRC defending China's
treatment of Uyghurs in the <color=#3366CC>Xinjiang</color> region.
In October 2020, President Emomali Rahmon was re-elected for another seven-year term with 90% of the vote,
following a largely ceremonial election.
In April 2021, a <color=#3366CC>conflict over water</color> with <color=#3366CC>Kyrgyzstan</color> escalated into one of the border clashes between the two countries
since independence.
In July 2021, Tajikistan appealed to members of a Russian-led <color=#3366CC>Collective Security Treaty Organization</color> (CSTO) of
ex-Soviet states for help in dealing with security challenges emerging from neighbouring <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>. The safety
concerns emerged as foreign troops such as the US and British army exited the country, causing over 1,000 Afghan
civilians and servicemen to flee to neighbouring Tajikistan after <color=#3366CC>Taliban</color> insurgents <color=#3366CC>took control of parts</color> of Afghanistan.
Administrative divisions
Tajikistan consists of four administrative divisions at the first level. These are the provinces (viloyat) of Sughd and
Khatlon, the autonomous province of Gorno-Badakhshan (abbreviated as GBAO), and the Regions of Republican
Subordination (RRP – Raiony Respublikanskogo Podchineniya in transliteration from Russian). The capital city,
<color=#3366CC>Dushanbe</color>, is administered separately as a city of republican subordination.
Each region is divided into districts ( or raion). As of 2024, there are 47 districts in Tajikistan (excluding the 4 city
districts within Dushanbe). The districts are further subdivided into jamoats (village-level self-governing units), which
are then divided into villages (qyshloqs). As of 2024, there are approximately 406 jamoats.
Economy
Tajikistan's economy has experienced significant growth in recent years, with real GDP expanding by 8.4% in 2024 and
maintaining a growth rate of 8.4% in 2025, reaching a nominal GDP of 176.9 billion somoni. Growth in the first half of
2025 averaged 8.1%. The World Bank projects growth to moderate to 6.2% in 2026 and 4.7% in 2027, while the IMF
forecasts 6.0% for 2026. The government's own target for 2026 remains 8.5%.
In 2024, Tajikistan remained one of the world's most remittance-dependent economies, with remittances accounting for
approximately 49% of GDP, up from 39% in 2023. The World Bank estimated remittance inflows at $5.8 billion in 2024,
representing a 27% increase. In the first quarter of 2025, remittances surged by 62.9% in dollar terms compared to the
same period in 2024, driven primarily by higher wages for migrant workers in Russia. However, the World Bank has
warned that a downturn in the Russian economy could lead to returning migrants facing limited economic prospects at
home.
Inflation has declined to historic lows, averaging 3.6% in 2024 and 3.5% in 2025—the lowest since independence.
Food prices rose by 4.5%, services by 5.7%, and non-food goods by 1.5% in 2025. The National Bank of Tajikistan
targets an inflation range of 3–7%, while the World Bank projects inflation at 4.5% for 2026.
Poverty has declined substantially, with the national poverty rate falling from 56% in 2010 to approximately 20% in
2024. The middle class grew from 8% to 33% over the same period. Under the lower-middle-income country poverty
line ($4.20 per day in 2017 PPP), 16.9% of the population lived in poverty in 2024. Despite these gains, the World Bank
notes that poverty reduction has been driven primarily by wage growth and remittances rather than domestic job
creation. Labour force participation remains low at only 40%—the lowest in Central Asia—with female participation at
just 21%.
The primary sources of income in Tajikistan remain aluminium production, cotton growing, and remittances from
migrant workers. The state-owned Tajik Aluminum Company (TadAZ) produced 83,000 tonnes of aluminium in 2024,
representing a 24% increase, with a target of 180,000 tonnes for 2025. Aluminium exports reached 71,110 tonnes in
2024, a 36.5% increase, though the sector accounts for only 1.33% of industrial output.
Cotton production, however, has declined sharply from 404,700 tonnes in 2022 to 253,200 tonnes in 2024. Fibre
exports totalled 100,500 tonnes worth $170.1 million in 2024, with Iran receiving 67.9%, Turkey 15%, and China 8.4%.
Cotton no longer accounts for 60% of agricultural output as previously reported, reflecting a significant restructuring of
the agricultural sector.
Gold production grew by 18.8% in 2024, though exports of precious metals fell by 69.6% due to reduced gold
shipments.
Tajikistan's hydropower potential remains a key focus, with the <color=#3366CC>Rogun Dam</color> project progressing. The World Bank
approved $350 million in financing in late 2024, and the OPEC Fund provided a $25 million loan for construction. Once
completed, the 335-metre dam will be the tallest in the world, with a capacity of 3,780 MW. The <color=#3366CC>Nurek Dam</color>, currently
the second highest dam in the world, remains operational. Other hydroelectric projects include the Sangtuda-1 and
Sangtuda-2 stations. Russia's RAO UES completed Sangtuda-1 (670 MW capacity) which commenced operations in
January 2008. Iran has been involved in Sangtuda-2, and Chinese company SinoHydro has worked on the Zerafshan
project.
The planned CASA-1000 project aims to transmit 1,000 MW of surplus electricity from Tajikistan to Pakistan via
Afghanistan. The 750 km transmission line is being developed as a public-private partnership with support from the
World Bank, IFC, ADB, and IDB, with an estimated cost of approximately US$865 million. Other energy resources
include coal deposits and smaller reserves of natural gas and petroleum.
The unemployment rate remains a subject of debate, with official registered unemployment at approximately 50,900
people (June 2025), while international estimates from the World Bank place the rate at approximately 11.6% (2024).
This discrepancy reflects the large informal economy and underemployment not captured in official figures.
Drug trafficking remains an illegal source of income, with Tajikistan serving as a transit country for Afghan narcotics
bound for Russian and European markets. The UNODC continues to work with Tajik authorities to strengthen border
controls, provide training, and establish joint interdiction teams. The Tajikistani Drug Control Agency has been
established with international support. However, according to some experts, drug money has contributed to corruption
at various levels of government. Tajikistan ranks among the leading countries globally for heroin and raw opium
confiscations, though recent figures have not been publicly updated from earlier records.
China has become a significant economic partner under the <color=#3366CC>Belt and Road Initiative</color>, with total Chinese investment in
Tajikistan reaching approximately $4.1 billion between 2007 and 2023. Over 700 Chinese companies operate in the
country, spanning infrastructure, mining, energy, and manufacturing sectors.
The World Bank's 2025 assessment notes that while Tajikistan has made significant progress in economic growth and
poverty reduction, the economy remains vulnerable to external shocks, particularly fluctuations in remittance flows from
Russia and changes in global commodity prices. Diversification away from reliance on remittances, aluminium, and
cotton remains a key policy challenge.
Telecommunications
Tajikistan's communications market grew 13.7% in 2025 to 4.9 billion somoni.
Average mobile internet speed increased from 7.2 Mbps at the beginning of 2025 to 35.4 Mbps in 2026. Fixed internet
speed increased from 30 Mbps to over 40 Mbps in 2025, with plans to reach 100 Mbps within two years. Average
internet consumption per user has increased tenfold over the past five years, from 3 to 30 GB. Fixed internet prices
have decreased by an average of 55%.
Tajikistan is in the early stages of 5G deployment. A memorandum on the establishment of a national 5G consortium
was signed between the Communications Service and the country's mobile operators—Indigo Tajikistan, TT Mobile,
Babilon M, Tacom, and Tojiktelecom—to coordinate the rollout of next-generation mobile technologies. Currently, 84
5G base stations are active.
In October 2025, a licensing agreement was signed with Starlink Tajikistan (SpaceX), enabling the launch of Starlink
operations in the country.
Transportation
As a landlocked country, Tajikistan has no ports, and the majority of transportation is via road, air, and rail. In 2025, the
country had an ambitious agenda to modernize its transport sector, focusing on infrastructure upgrades and stronger
international connections. As of 2026, the country is implementing 11 investment projects in the road and transport
sector with a total value of USD 1.193 billion. Under the State Budget for 2025, nearly 3 billion somoni ($274.35 million)
was allocated to the transport and communications sector.
The government has pursued agreements with Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan to gain access to ports and establish
regional transit corridors. In July 2026, Iran, Afghanistan, and Tajikistan signed a trilateral transit corridor agreement to
activate a new road transit route. Afghanistan, Iran, and Turkey agreed to jointly construct a railway between Herat and
Mazar-i-Sharif in 2025. Tajikistan has also been exploring participation in the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway
project.
In 2025, a total of 154.8 million tons of cargo were transported by all modes of transport, which is 15.2 percent more
compared to 2024. In 2025, road transport carried 147.3 million tons of cargo and 1,129.5 million passengers.
Road
<color=#3366CC>Road transport</color> continues to dominate Tajikistan's transport system, accounting for more than 90% of passenger
transportation and over 80% of domestic freight. As of 2025, the total length of roads in the country is approximately
27,800 kilometres. In 2025, through state investment projects, 236 kilometers of roads and other transport
infrastructure facilities were built and put into operation, with an investment of 5.4 billion somoni (about $580 million).
Currently, there are 16 transport sector projects under construction nationwide, with a total investment of about 11.3
billion somoni (about $1.22 billion).
Major road projects completed or underway include:
The construction of the <color=#3366CC>Rogun reservoir</color> affected the Obigarm–Nurobod section of the M41 highway. The 75-kilometer
Rogun–Obigarm–Nurobod International Highway was opened in August 2025, bypassing the Rogun reservoir. The
project includes three tunnels—"35th Anniversary of Independence" (2,605 m), "Vahdat" (1,700 m), and "Oriyono"
(1,600 m)—which shorten the route by 24 km, as well as 14 bridges spanning approximately 1,150 meters. This route
connects the capital with the administrative centers of the Nurobod, Rasht, Sangvor, Tojikobod and Lakhsh districts,
expanding communication in all directions, including trade turnover between Tajikistan and <color=#3366CC>Kyrgyzstan</color> and regional
transit. In June 2025, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank approved a $2.04 million grant—its first under a
Project-Specific Window—to support restoration of the 75-kilometer stretch.
The launch of the Dangara–Guliston Green Corridor project (49 km) began in March 2025, upgrading the road from two
to four lanes and adding bike lanes, sidewalks, lighting, crossings, and electric vehicle charging stations. Financing
comes from a mixture of international sources, including a <color=#3366CC>European Bank for Reconstruction and Development</color>
(EBRD) loan of up to €38 million and an <color=#3366CC>Asian Development Bank</color> (ADB) grant of up to $86.7 million, with completion
expected by 2030.
The Dushanbe–Chanak highway (358 km), connecting the capital to the <color=#3366CC>Uzbekistan</color> border, continues to undergo
maintenance and reconstruction. As of August 2025, approximately 347,000 tons of asphalt had been used in its repair
since 2012. The route includes three tunnels—"Maikhura" (897 m), "Istiklol" (4,998 m), and "Shakhristan" (5,253
m)—as well as 38 bridges and 24 avalanche galleries.
The Qalaikhumb–Vanj–Rushan section of the Dushanbe–Kulob–Khorog–Kulma highway was completed in 2025,
funded by a $230 million grant from the Chinese government. President <color=#3366CC>Emomali Rahmon</color> inaugurated a section of the
Kulob–Khorog–Kulma–China highway in 2025.
In February 2025, Tajikistan signed an agreement with China's Zhejiang Communications Construction Group to build
<color=#3366CC>Central Asia</color>'s longest road bridge over the Surkhab River. The bridge will span 920 meters (1,500 meters including
access roads) and is expected to be completed within four years at a cost of nearly $60 million. The bridge will be the
largest road bridge in the republic in terms of design and style.
Tajikistan and China have agreed to build 93 km of roads and two tunnels (total length 5.2 km) as part of a broader
infrastructure partnership. The project includes five avalanche corridors totaling 602 meters, 15 bridges totaling 633
meters, 21,850 meters of protective walls, and 151 artificial structures. In September 2025, the governments of
Tajikistan and China signed an agreement on international road transportation, along with seven other supplementary
instruments in Beijing, encompassing various domains of bilateral collaboration.
China has resumed construction of a strategic 109-kilometer section of the Dushanbe–Kulma Highway near the Afghan
border after several months of suspension, following new security guarantees provided by the Tajik government.
Construction resumed in April 2026 after Tajik authorities introduced enhanced security measures to protect Chinese
engineers and workers. The project had been suspended in late 2025 following a series of violent attacks on Chinese
nationals.
In December 2025, Tajikistan and Kuwaiti consulting company NARCO signed an agreement for the rehabilitation of
the 162-kilometer Ayni–Kuhistoni Mastchoh road in Sughd province. The project includes road surface modernization,
widening of the roadway, the construction of 27 bridges and 405 culverts, and the updating of engineering systems.
In 2026, eight new road projects with a total length of nearly 286.9 km and a combined value of USD 334.9 million are
scheduled to begin, including the rehabilitation of the Guliston–Kulob road (32.2 km, USD 80 million),
Baljuvon–Sarikhosor road (58 km, USD 58 million), the Murghab–Kulma section (67 km, USD 78 million), construction
of three bridges on the Labijar–Sangvor route (USD 17.1 million), construction of the Kulob bypass road (11 km, USD
30 million), rehabilitation of the Vahdat–Obigarm road (70 km, USD 28.8 million), construction of the
Khistevarz–Konibodom (Arka) road (9.7 km, USD 4.5 million), and the Khorugh–Roshtqala road (39 km, USD 38.5
million).
The Tajik–Afghan Friendship Bridge, built by the United States in 2004, remains an important link connecting Tajikistan
to Afghanistan and South Asia.
Tajikistan faces significant challenges in maintaining its road infrastructure. According to the Asian Transport
Observatory, the country faces estimated average annual losses of $14.5 million to transport infrastructure, with 91% of
these losses concentrated in the road sector.
Rail
The railroad system consists of approximately 680 kilometres of broad gauge, non-electrified single-track lines.
According to Tajikistan's Ministry of Transport, the total length exceeds 980 kilometres, including approach and
technical tracks. In the first half of 2025, rail accounted for approximately 70% of international freight traffic. In 2025,
railway transport (including loading, dispatch, and transit shipments) carried 7.4 million tons of cargo, which is 10.9
percent more than in 2024. The network consists of three disconnected segments (northern, central, and southern),
which require transit through Uzbekistan and <color=#3366CC>Turkmenistan</color> for interconnection.
The principal segments are in the southern region, connecting the capital with the industrial areas of the Hisor and
Vakhsh valleys, and with Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan, and Russia. The Bokhtar–Kulob railway connects the
Kulob District with the central area of the country. The Vahdat–Yavan railway (48.65 km) is another important line,
connecting the Districts of Republican Subordination with Khatlon region.
Railway development in 2025 centered on electrification plans and regional integration. Tajik Railways began
preliminary work on electrifying the 62-kilometer Vahdat–Pakhtaobod line, which links eastern Dushanbe with the
Uzbek border. This section of the line serves a commuter train that runs daily between Dushanbe-1 station and
Pakhtaobod, with 15 intermediate stops. The travel time is approximately one hour. Authorities also explored
electrification of the Kanibadam–Bekabad route. Feasibility studies continued for a proposed 51-kilometer railway
connecting Jaloliddini Balkhi with Nizhniy Pyandzh, discussed within cooperation frameworks involving South Korea.
Tajikistan has also been examining possible participation in the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway project, which is
expected to span more than 530 kilometers and include 20 stations.
Iran and Tajikistan have commenced a new chapter aimed at enhancing railway cooperation through the signing of a
memorandum of understanding (MoU), seeking to strengthen and expand railway trade. In July 2025, Afghanistan,
Uzbekistan, and Pakistan signed an agreement to begin a feasibility study for the "Afghan-Trans" railway project.
Air
Tajikistan had 26 airports in 2009, of which 18 had paved runways, with two having runways longer than 3,000 metres.
In 2025, Tajikistan's international airports served 2,963,000 passengers, marking a 21% increase compared to 2024.
Major airports include:
• Dushanbe International Airport – the country's main hub, featuring a 3,100-metre main runway capable of
accommodating Boeing 737s and Airbus A320s. In 2025, construction began on a new 1,500-metre taxiway and 10
additional parking lots for large aircraft as part of an "Open Skies" policy. The "Open Skies" policy, introduced in
June 2025, abolished the previous principle of flight parity, which limited the number of flights operated by foreign
airlines, equating them to the number of flights operated by domestic carriers. A new terminal is also under
construction at Dushanbe International Airport, with Turkish specialists preparing the design documentation and the
facility scheduled to open within one to two years. In December 2025, President Rahmon ordered the renovation of
the international airports of Dushanbe, Bokhtar, and Kulob to bring them into line with modern service standards.
• Khujand Airport – features a single runway measuring 3,185 metres in length and 50 metres in width.
• Kulob Airport – features a single asphalt runway measuring 3,000 metres in length and 42 metres in width.
Electric vehicles and green mobility
Tajikistan has seen a dramatic increase in electric vehicle (EV) adoption. As of June 2025, the number of registered
EVs exceeded 34,000 units, representing more than 5% of the country's total vehicle fleet. This shift has contributed to
a reduction of 18,500 tons in liquefied gas imports in the first half of 2025. Since April 2025, Tajikistan has exempted
new EVs (less than one year old) from import customs duties.
Urban transport
Urban transport modernization gained momentum in 2025, particularly in the capital Dushanbe. Tajikistan announced
plans to begin work on a light metro system in Dushanbe, with a feasibility study scheduled for completion in 2025 and
construction planned between 2028 and 2033. The first underground line will span 10.5 kilometres, linking the southern
gate of the capital (Darvozai) with central areas.
The EBRD is supporting the reconstruction of Dushanbe's road infrastructure through a newly established Road
Reconstruction Project Implementation Group under the Ministry of Transport. Tajikistan and China have also agreed to
step up work on the construction of two-level road interchanges in Dushanbe.
As of September 2025, Dushanbe's public transport fleet increased by 20%, reaching 380 buses, 65 trolleybuses, and
over 1,100 minibuses. Additionally, 60 electric buses operate on 8 city routes, with plans to increase this number to 90
units. Authorities had planned a full transition of Dushanbe's taxi fleet to electric vehicles by September 2025, though
while significant progress was made, the deadline was not fully met.
In the Sughd region, a new 12.7-kilometre section of the Dehmoy–Konibodom road is planned at a cost of over $8
million, with 11 road bridges and 17 bus stops already constructed along the route.
Regional and international cooperation
Tajikistan has been actively pursuing regional transport integration. In July 2026, Iran, Afghanistan, and Tajikistan
signed a trilateral transit corridor agreement in Mashhad, establishing a joint road transit corridor aimed at boosting
regional trade. Under the agreement, a new transit route connecting the three countries will be activated, with the first
trial cargo shipment expected within one month. The agreement also includes the formation of a joint working group
tasked with addressing administrative obstacles, facilitating visas for drivers, reducing border delays and developing
shared insurance mechanisms.
China has become a significant economic partner under the <color=#3366CC>Belt and Road Initiative</color>, with total Chinese investment in
Tajikistan reaching approximately $4.1 billion between 2007 and 2023. Over 700 Chinese companies operate in the
country, spanning infrastructure, mining, energy, and manufacturing sectors. Following the signing of a friendship treaty
between China and Tajikistan in May, approximately $8 billion in economic and infrastructure agreements were signed,
expanding cooperation in transport, infrastructure and security.
Tajikistan and Kazakhstan are also expanding transport cooperation, with road freight transportation between the two
countries increasing during the first four months of 2026, with total cargo volumes rising 5.8% and the number of
vehicles increasing 17.9% compared with the same period last year.
Challenges and vulnerabilities
Tajikistan's transport sector faces several significant challenges. According to the Asian Transport Observatory, the
country faces estimated average annual losses of $14.5 million to transport infrastructure, with 91% of these losses
concentrated in the road sector. Greenhouse gas emissions from road transport are growing at an annual rate of
Security concerns have impacted infrastructure projects, as demonstrated by the suspension of the Dushanbe–Kulma
Highway project following attacks on Chinese nationals. Out of 225 registered transport companies, only 107 have their
own material and technical base, with the rest operating through leasing arrangements, affecting service quality.
Traffic congestion in Dushanbe remains a major concern, with the Minister of Transport ordering urgent measures in
October 2025, including the completion of a comprehensive road infrastructure inventory, the development of a digital
road map, the use of digital technology and artificial intelligence, and the transition to cashless payment systems
across all transport services by the end of 2025. Proposed solutions include restrictions on personal vehicle use,
congestion charges on central streets, installation of smart traffic lights, development of paid parking, construction of
multi-storey parking facilities, stricter regulations on taxis, and dedicated bus lanes.
The transport sector's budget allocation has been reduced by 24% in the 2025–2027 program, potentially limiting the
pace of infrastructure development. Additionally, the Istiklol Tunnel project faced suspension due to a $2.16 million
funding shortfall from Iran.
Despite these challenges, Tajikistan continues to pursue an ambitious transport modernization agenda, with multiple
international partners supporting road rehabilitation, railway electrification, airport upgrades, and the development of
sustainable urban transport solutions.
Demographics
In 2023, Tajikistan was estimated to have a population of 10,389,799, according to <color=#3366CC>World Bank</color> data. The Tajiks, who
speak <color=#3366CC>Tajik</color>, are the main ethnic group, while there are minorities of Uzbeks and Russians, whose numbers are
declining owing to emigration. This makes Tajikistan the only country in Central Asia to have a minority of Turkic people
and a majority of Iranic people. The Pamiris of <color=#3366CC>Badakhshan</color>, the Yaghnobi people, and a minority of <color=#3366CC>Ismailis</color> are
considered to belong to the larger group of Tajiks. Citizens of Tajikistan are called Tajikistanis.
In 1989, ethnic Russians in Tajikistan made up 7.6% of the population; by 1998, the proportion had fallen to
approximately 0.5% following the <color=#3366CC>Tajikistani Civil War</color>, which had displaced the majority of ethnic Russians. After the
end of the war, Russian emigration continued. The ethnic German population of Tajikistan has also declined owing to
emigration: having peaked at 38,853 in 1979, it has "almost vanished" since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
The Tajiks are the principal ethnic group in most of Tajikistan and in northern and western <color=#3366CC>Afghanistan</color>; there are more
Tajiks in Afghanistan than in Tajikistan. Tajiks are a minority in <color=#3366CC>Uzbekistan</color>. Approximately 2.4 million Tajik citizens
were officially registered in Russia in 2021.
Languages
The official <color=#3366CC>languages</color> of Tajikistan are <color=#3366CC>Tajik</color> as the state language and <color=#3366CC>Russian</color> as the interethnic language, as
understood in Article 2 of the Constitution: "The state language of Tajikistan shall be Tajik. Russian shall be the
language of international communication."
The state (national) language of the Republic of Tajikistan is <color=#3366CC>Tajik</color>, which is written in the Tajik Cyrillic alphabet. Millions
of native Tajik speakers live in neighbouring <color=#3366CC>Uzbekistan</color> and in Russia.
According to article 2 of the Constitution of the Republic of Tajikistan, Russian is recognised as the second official
language of Tajikistan; the official language of inter-ethnic communication in the country.
Approximately 90% of the population of Tajikistan speaks Russian at varying levels. The varieties of Russian spoken in
Tajikistan are referred to by scholars as Tajik(istani) Russian and it shares some similarities with Uzbek(istani) Russian,
such as morphological differences and lexical differences such as the use of word for a wild apricot or for rhubarb.
Both Russian and Tajik speakers in the country use the following words in common in addressing unfamiliar people and
acquaintances.
The "highly educated" part of the population of Tajikistan, and the intelligentsia, prefer to speak Russian and Persian,
the pronunciation of which in Tajikistan is called the "Iranian style".
Native Uzbek speakers live in the north and west of Tajikistan. In fourth place (after Tajik, Russian and Uzbek) by
number of native speakers are Pamir languages, whose native speakers live in Kuhistani Badakshshan Autonomous
Region. The majority of <color=#3366CC>Zoroastrians</color> in Tajikistan speak one of the Pamir languages. Native speakers of the <color=#3366CC>Kyrgyz</color>
<color=#3366CC>language</color> live in the north of Kuhistani Badakshshan Autonomous Region. Yagnobi language speakers live in the west
of the country. The Parya language of local <color=#3366CC>Romani people</color> is spoken in Tajikistan. Tajikistan has communities of native

speakers of <color=#3366CC>Persian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pashto</color>, <color=#3366CC>Armenian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Azerbaijani</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tatar</color>, <color=#3366CC>Turkmen</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kazakh</color>, <color=#3366CC>Chinese</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Ukrainian</color>.
Religion
Tajikistan is a secular state with a constitution providing for freedom of religion, but nevertheless it heavily regulates the
practices of its Muslim majority. Sunni Islam of the <color=#3366CC>Hanafi</color> school has been officially recognised by the government
since 2009. The government has declared two Islamic holidays, <color=#3366CC>Eid ul-Fitr</color> and <color=#3366CC>Eid al-Adha</color>, as state holidays.
According to a <color=#3366CC>US State Department</color> release and Pew research group, the population of Tajikistan is 98% <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color>.
Approximately 87–95% of them are <color=#3366CC>Sunni</color> and roughly 3% are <color=#3366CC>Shia</color> and roughly 7% are non-denominational Muslims.
The Shia part of the population predominantly live in the Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Region and are followers of
the <color=#3366CC>Ismaili</color> branch of Shia Islam. The remaining 2% of the population are followers of <color=#3366CC>Russian Orthodoxy</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Protestantism</color>, <color=#3366CC>Zoroastrianism</color> and <color=#3366CC>Buddhism</color>. Muslims fast during Ramadan, while about one third in the countryside
and 10% in the cities observe daily prayer and dietary restrictions.
As of January 2016, as part of an "anti-radicalisation campaign", police in the Khatlon region reportedly shaved the
beards of 13,000 men and shut down 160 shops selling the <color=#3366CC>hijab</color>. Shaving beards and discouraging women from
wearing hijabs is part of a government campaign targeting trends that are deemed "alien and inconsistent with Tajik
culture", and "to preserve secular traditions".
There is a concern for religious institutions becoming active in the political sphere. The Islamic Renaissance Party
(IRP), a combatant in the <color=#3366CC>1992–1997 Civil War</color> and then-proponent of the creation of an <color=#3366CC>Islamic state</color> in Tajikistan,
constitutes no more than 30% of the government by statute. Membership in <color=#3366CC>Hizb ut-Tahrir</color>, a militant Islamic party
which aims for an overthrow of secular governments and the unification of Tajiks under one Islamic state, is illegal and
members are subject to arrest and imprisonment.
By law, religious communities must register with the State Committee on Religious Affairs (SCRA) and with local
authorities. Registration with the SCRA requires a charter, a list of ten or more members, and evidence of local
government approval for the prayer site location. Religious groups that do not have a physical structure are not allowed
to gather publicly for prayer. Failure to register can result in fines and closure of a place of worship. There are reports
that registration at the local level is sometimes difficult to obtain. People under the age of 18 are barred from public
religious practice.
Approximately 1.6% of the population in Tajikistan is <color=#3366CC>Christian</color>, mostly <color=#3366CC>Orthodox Christians</color>. The territory of Tajikistan is
part of the of the of the <color=#3366CC>Russian Orthodox Moscow Patriarchate</color>. The country is home to communities of <color=#3366CC>Catholics</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Armenian Christians</color>, <color=#3366CC>Protestants</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lutherans</color>, <color=#3366CC>Jehovah's Witnesses</color>, <color=#3366CC>Baptists</color>, Mormons, and Adventists.
Bukharan Jews have lived in Tajikistan since the 2nd century BC. In the 1940s, the Jewish community of Tajikistan
numbered nearly 30,000 people. Most were Persianspeaking Bukharan Jews who had lived in the region for millennia,
along with Ashkenazi Jews from Eastern Europe who resettled there in the Soviet era. As of 2011, the Jewish
population was estimated at fewer than 500, with roughly half living in <color=#3366CC>Dushanbe</color>.
Education
An estimated 99.8% of the population of Tajikistan have the ability to read and write.
Public education in Tajikistan consists of 11 years of primary and secondary education and the government planned to
implement a 12-year system in 2016. There are a number of tertiary education institutions including Khujand State
University, which has 76 departments in 15 faculties, Tajikistan State University of Law, Business, & Politics, Khorugh
State University, Agricultural University of Tajikistan, Tajik National University, and other institutions. Universities were
established during the Soviet Era. As of 2008 tertiary education enrollment was 17%, below the sub-regional average
of 37%, while higher than any other low-income country after <color=#3366CC>Syria</color>. Tajiks left the education system due to "low"
demand in the labour market for people with "extensive" educational training or professional skills.
Public spending on education was relatively constant between 2005–2012 and fluctuated from 3.5% to 4.1% of <color=#3366CC>GDP</color>
below the <color=#3366CC>OECD</color> average of 6%. The <color=#3366CC>United Nations</color> reported that the level of spending was "severely inadequate to
meet the requirements of the country's high-needs education system."
According to a UNICEF-supported survey, about 25% of girls in Tajikistan fail to complete compulsory primary
education because of poverty and gender bias, while <color=#3366CC>literacy</color> is "generally high" in Tajikistan. Estimates of out of school
children range from 4.6% to 19.4% with the majority being girls.
In September 2017, the University of Central Asia launched its second campus in Khorog, Tajikistan, offering majors in
Earth & Environmental Sciences and Economics. Tajikistan was ranked 108th in the Global Innovation Index in 2025.
Science in the territory of Tajikistan achieved "success" in the Middle Ages, and scientific organisations were created in
the Soviet period. During the period of independence, the scientific sphere has experienced a "crisis": the annual
number of patent applications for inventions decreased in 1994–2011 from 193 to 5. A contribution to science is made
by universities, where in 2011 6707 researchers worked, of which 2450 had academic degrees.
Employment
In 2009 nearly 1 million Tajiks worked abroad (mainly in Russia). More than 70% of the female population lives in
traditional villages.
Health
The state's Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare reported that 104,272 disabled people were registered in Tajikistan in
2000. The government of Tajikistan and the World Bank considered activities to support this part of the population, as
described in the World Bank's Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper. Public expenditure on health was 1% of GDP in
<color=#3366CC>Life expectancy</color> at birth was estimated at 69 years in 2020. The <color=#3366CC>infant mortality</color> rate was approximately 30.42 deaths
per 1,000 live births in 2018. In 2014, there were 2.1 physicians per 1,000 people, higher than in any other lowincome
country except <color=#3366CC>North Korea</color>.
Tajikistan has experienced a decrease in hospital beds per capita since 1992, following the dissolution of the <color=#3366CC>USSR</color>,
although the number remains at 4.8 beds per 1,000 people, above the world average of 2.7.
According to the World Bank, 96% of births are attended by skilled health staff, up from 66.6% in 1999.
In 2010, the country experienced an outbreak of <color=#3366CC>polio</color> that caused more than 457 cases in both children and adults and
resulted in 29 deaths, before being brought under control.
In the summer of 2021, the coronavirus ravaged the country, and the Tajik president's sister reportedly died of
<color=#3366CC>COVID-19</color> in a hospital. According to local media, the president's sister's sons physically assaulted the health minister
and a senior doctor.
In 2023, according to the <color=#3366CC>World Health Organization</color>, Tajikistan received certification declaring it a <color=#3366CC>malaria</color>free country.
Culture
The culture of Tajikistan has developed over several thousand years. Tajik culture can be divided into two areas,
Metropolitan and Kuhiston (Highland). Modern city centres include <color=#3366CC>Dushanbe</color> (the capital), <color=#3366CC>Khujand</color>, Kulob, and
Panjakent.
The <color=#3366CC>Tajik language</color> is the mother tongue of around 80% of the citizens of Tajikistan. There are Uzbek, Kyrgyz and
Russian minorities. The Yaghnobi people live in areas of northern Tajikistan. The estimated number of Yaghnobis is
about 25,000. Forced migrations in the 20th century decimated their numbers. They speak the Yaghnobi language,
which is the only direct descendant of the Sogdian language and has often been called Neo-Sogdian in academic
literature.
Tajikistan artisans created the Dushanbe Tea House, which was presented in 1988 as a gift to the sister city of
Boulder, Colorado.
In the country, especially among women from the indigenous population, the wearing of traditional national clothing is
preserved. The seamstresses and embroiderers of regions of Tajikistan use factory fabrics and local needlework
embroidery for home decoration and women's clothing. The practice of Chakan embroidery is preserved among women
in certain areas, passing the knowledge down from one generation to the next.
Festivals and national holidays
Tajikistan celebrates several ancient national holidays that form the core of its cultural identity. These include <color=#3366CC>Nowruz</color>,
Mehrgon, Sada, and Tirgon, which are recognized as the most valuable elements of Tajik intangible cultural heritage.
Nowruz is the most important holiday in Tajikistan, marking the spring equinox, the beginning of the solar year, and the
New Year on the Iranian calendar. Nowruz, meaning "New Day," heralds the arrival of spring and is observed annually
on March 21, the vernal equinox. The celebration traces back over 6,000 years, with historical ties to the <color=#3366CC>Silk Road</color>. In
2026, Dushanbe was selected as the main center for international Nowruz celebrations. The International Festival
"Nowruz – Cultural and Global Heritage" is held annually during the third decade of March. The holiday is celebrated
from 21 to 24 March, with government employees receiving a total of 10 days off.
Mehrgon is an ancient harvest festival rooted in <color=#3366CC>Zoroastrian</color> traditions, dedicated to the deity Mehr (<color=#3366CC>Mithra</color>). In the
ancient Persian calendar, Mehrgon fell in mid-autumn, symbolizing the end of agricultural work and a time to thank the
gods for prosperity. It was revived in 2009 by presidential decree and added to Tajikistan's national list of intangible
cultural heritage in 2017.
Sada is one of the oldest holidays of the Tajik people, symbolizing the approach of Nowruz and the arrival of spring.
According to scholars, Sada falls fifty nights and fifty days before Nowruz and serves as a reminder to farmers to
prepare for the spring sowing. The name "Sada" is usually associated with the number one hundred, or fifty days and
fifty nights, before Nowruz. In December 2023, the joint nomination of Tajikistan and Iran for the "Sada Festival" was
inscribed on <color=#3366CC>UNESCO's</color> Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Tirgon is another ancient festival that, along with Sada, Navruz, and Mehrgon, is celebrated as part of Tajikistan's rich
cultural heritage.
Cultural infrastructure
In 2025, 44 cultural facilities were built in Tajikistan, while 120 facilities—including libraries, cultural centres, museums,
parks, and music schools—were fully renovated and reconstructed. The Ministry of Culture participated in 65
international scientific and cultural events across 21 countries.
The National Theatre of Tajikistan is under construction in Dushanbe, adjacent to the National Museum and the
National Flag Park. The building will have 2 underground and 5 above-ground floors, reaching a height of 34.5 meters.
A State Program for the Development of Performing Arts for 2025–2029 has been approved, with more than 14 million
somoni allocated for theatre development.
The State Academic Opera and Ballet Theatre named after Sadriddin Aini signed a cooperation memorandum with the
Karaganda Academic Musical Comedy Theatre (Kazakhstan) in September 2025, with plans for performances in Rome
Literature
Tajik literature has a rich history dating back over a thousand years. <color=#3366CC>Rudaki</color> (858–941 CE), known as the "Adam of
Poets," is considered a father of classical Persian literature and takes centre stage in Tajikistan's literary heritage. He is
regarded as the first major poet to write in New Persian. Although only a small portion of his work has survived, his
influence on Persian and Tajik poetry remains profound.
Sadriddin Aini (1878–1954) is regarded as the founder of modern Tajik literature. He was a poet, writer, historian,
translator, scholar, and political figure. Aini excelled in research and literary criticism, and his papers on the lives and
works of Rudaki are particularly notable.
In 2025, Tajikistan participated in the 36th Tehran International Book Fair with more than 400 newly published titles.
Works by classical poets such as Rudaki, <color=#3366CC>Ferdowsi</color>, Hafez, Saadi, Bidel, and Jami, as well as contemporary writers like
Mirzo Tursunzoda, Layeq Shir-Ali, Mu'min Qanoat, Gulrukhsor, and Muhammad Ghoyib, were presented. The Persian
translation of Sadriddin Aini's novel Odina was published in Iran in 2025. A collection of poems titled Kamandi Zulf by
Zulfiya Atoi, a folk poet of Tajikistan, was published by the ECO Cultural Institute in <color=#3366CC>Tehran</color>.
Visual arts and handicrafts
Chakan embroidery is a distinctive form of Tajik embroidery that was inscribed in 2018 on UNESCO's Representative
List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The art of Chakan embroidery involves sewing ornaments, images
of flowers and symbolic drawings with colourful threads on cotton or silk fabrics. The National Festival "Sad Gul-i
Chakan" was held on 5 March 2025 at the Dushanbe Philharmonic Hall, with craftswomen from Sughd, Khatlon,
Badakhshan, and the Rasht valleys displaying their works.
Suzani embroidery is another important Tajik handicraft. Tajik masters embroidered suzani wall panels, zardevor
ceiling friezes, borpush, kars, ruidjo covers and blankets, joynamaz prayer mats, as well as chakan dresses. The city of
Panjakent was designated as a "World Craft City for Panjakent Suzani Embroidery" by the World Crafts Council on 21
October 2025.
In September 2025, the exhibition "The World of Tajik Embroidery" opened at the Azerbaijan National Carpet Museum,
featuring 56 unique pieces from the Golden Treasury of the National Museum of Tajikistan. The exhibition included
suzani embroidery, chakan dresses, popurduzi embroidery, blankets, prayer rugs, embroidered men's waistbands
(miyonband), mirror covers (oinakhalta), wall embroidery, and tablecloths.
Music and performing arts
Tajikistan has a rich musical heritage, with two genres – Shashmaqom and Falak – recognized as masterpieces of
intangible cultural heritage.
Shashmaqom is the basis of Tajik traditional music and the highest manifestation of the musical mind of the people.
Shashmaqom, meaning "six maqoms", constitutes a fusion of vocal and instrumental music, melodic and rhythmic
idioms and poetry. The system of musical grammar of professional traditional Tajik music has been formed on the basis
of maqoms. The six maqoms are Buzurg, Rost, Navo, Dugoh, Segoh, and Iroq. The poetic texts of the vocal sections
are drawn from the works of classical Persian-Tajik poets such as <color=#3366CC>Hafez</color>, <color=#3366CC>Saadi</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Jami</color>. Traditional instruments
accompanying Shashmaqom include the tanbur, dutar, and doira. The musical genre emerged in the pre-Islamic period
in <color=#3366CC>Bukhara</color> and later spread throughout the Eastern world. In 2003, Shashmaqom was inscribed on UNESCO's
Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. May 12 is celebrated in Tajikistan as "Shashmaqom
Day." In June 2025, a Shashmaqom cultural program was held in Paris to mark the 700th anniversary of Hafez Sherazi
and the 60th anniversary of UNESCO's water sciences.
Falak is a musical genre consisting of a cycle of folk songs, accompanied by string musical instruments such as the
dumbra, tablak, and ghizhak. Falak, meaning 'heaven', 'fortune' and 'universe', is the traditional folklore music of the
mountain people of Tajikistan. The expressive and philosophical musical genre may be performed by a male or female
soloist, either a cappella, or with a single instrumental accompaniment or an ensemble and dancers. It is performed in
the Khatlon region, Badakhshan, and the Rasht valley. In October 2025, an international symposium titled "Falak and
State Independence – from Revival to Global Recognition" was held in Dushanbe to comprehensively examine Falak
as a unique phenomenon in Tajikistan's musical culture and its role in strengthening national identity.
Other traditional musical genres include Rubobnavozi (skill of playing the rubab), Qonunnavozi (skill of playing the
qonun), and Amiri (folk songs and melodies performed at celebrations and concerts).
Cinema
The second Dushanbe International Film Festival "Toji Somon" was held from 15 to 20 October 2025 under the motto
"History of the Development of Tajiks." Filmmakers from 20 countries participated. The film Black Rabbit, White Rabbit
directed by Shahram Mokri (Iran) was selected as Tajikistan's submission for the Best International Feature Film
category at the Oscars.
Cuisine
Tajik cuisine is hearty, filling, and rooted in Central Asian and Persian influences.
<color=#3366CC>Oshi Palav</color> (pilaf) is the national dish in Tajikistan. It is a rice dish made with shredded yellow turnip or carrots, pieces
of meat, all fried together in vegetable oil or mutton fat in a special qazan (a wok-shaped cauldron) over an open flame.
There are up to 200 varieties of the dish. Oshi palav is prepared for regular mealtimes, as well as social gatherings,
celebrations, and rituals. In 2016, Oshi Palav was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural
Heritage of Humanity.
Qurutob is a traditional dish made from pieces of flatbread soaked in yoghurt or dried curd sauce, topped with onions
and herbs. Other traditional dishes include mantu (steamed dumplings), shurbo and piti (meat and vegetable soups),
laghman and ugro (noodle soups), and sambusa (stuffed pastries). Traditional meals typically begin with dried fruits,
nuts, and halva, proceed to soups and meat dishes, and conclude with plov.
Sport
The national sport of Tajikistan is gushtigiri, a traditional form of <color=#3366CC>wrestling</color>. The sport has seen significant development
in recent years. The first edition of a national team club competition was held on 5 October 2025, with the participation
of 98 athletes from 14 sports clubs nationwide. According to the International Gushtingiri Federation's operational
calendar, the World Club Championships are scheduled for December 2026. The Tajikistan Gushtingiri Federation was
awarded as the "Best Non-Olympic Sports Federation".
The sixth international Gushtingiri tournament for the Dushanbe Mayor's Cup was held on 26 April 2025, at the Tennis
Palace, bringing together wrestlers from more than 25 countries. The 2025 national championship was held on 22–23
February 2025 at the National University of Tajikistan, featuring 410 athletes competing across 7 men's and 5 women's
weight categories. The 2026 national championship is scheduled for 10–11 February 2026 in Dushanbe. Dushanbe will
host the second World Gushtingiri Championship on 15–16 August 2026, with a total prize fund of $400,000; winners in
each weight category will receive $20,000, silver medalists $10,000, and bronze medalists $5,000.
Another traditional sport is <color=#3366CC>buzkashi</color>, a game played on horseback, similar to <color=#3366CC>polo</color>. Buzkashi may be played as an
individual sport and as a team sport. The aim of the game is to grab a 50 kg dead goat, ride clear of the other players,
get back to the starting point and drop it in a designated circle. It is played at <color=#3366CC>Nowruz</color> celebrations. In 2025, buzkashi
was featured prominently during the Nowruz celebrations in Dushanbe.
Tajikistan has sent athletes to every <color=#3366CC>Summer Olympic Games</color> and four <color=#3366CC>Winter Olympic Games</color> since gaining
independence and has enjoyed limited success. At the 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris, Tajikistan was represented by
14 athletes (11 men and 3 women) across 6 sports. The country secured three bronze medals, finishing 79th among
206 participating nations. The medalists were judokas Somon Mahmadbekov (up to 81 kg) and Temur Rakhimov (over

Grover Cleveland
Stephen Grover Cleveland (March 18, 1837 – June 24, 1908) was the 22nd and 24th <color=#3366CC>president of the United States</color>,
serving from 1885 to 1889 and from 1893 to 1897. He was the first Democrat elected president after the <color=#3366CC>American Civil</color>
<color=#3366CC>War</color> and the first U.S. president to serve nonconsecutive terms.
Born in Caldwell, New Jersey, Cleveland was elected mayor of Buffalo in 1881 and governor of New York in 1882.
While governor, he closely cooperated with state assembly minority leader <color=#3366CC>Theodore Roosevelt</color> to pass reform
measures, winning national attention. He led the Bourbon Democrats, a pro-business movement opposed to high
tariffs, free silver, <color=#3366CC>inflation</color>, <color=#3366CC>imperialism</color>, and <color=#3366CC>subsidies</color> to businesses, farmers, or veterans. His crusade for political
reform and <color=#3366CC>fiscal conservatism</color> made him an icon for American conservatives of the time. Cleveland also won praise for
honesty, self-reliance, integrity, and commitment to <color=#3366CC>classical liberalism</color>. His fight against political corruption, patronage,
and bossism convinced many like-minded Republicans, called "Mugwumps", to cross party lines and support him in the
1884 presidential election, which he narrowly won against Republican <color=#3366CC>James G. Blaine</color>.
During his first presidency, Cleveland signed the Interstate Commerce Act of 1887, which made the <color=#3366CC>railroad industry</color>
the first industry subject to federal regulation by a regulatory body, and the Dawes Act, which subdivided <color=#3366CC>Native</color>
<color=#3366CC>American</color> tribal communal landholdings into individual allotments. This policy led to Native Americans ceding control of
about two-thirds of their land between 1887 and 1934. In the 1888 election, Cleveland won the popular vote but lost the
electoral college and therefore the election to <color=#3366CC>Benjamin Harrison</color>. He returned to New York City and joined a <color=#3366CC>law firm</color>.
In a rematch against Harrison for the 1892 election, Cleveland won both the popular vote and electoral college,
returning him to the White House. One month before his second presidency began, the <color=#3366CC>Panic of 1893</color> sparked a severe
national depression. An anti-imperialist, Cleveland opposed the push to annex Hawaii, launched an investigation into
<color=#3366CC>the 1893 coup</color> against Queen <color=#3366CC>Liliuokalani</color>, and called for her restoration. Cleveland intervened in the 1894 <color=#3366CC>Pullman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Strike</color> to keep the railroads moving, angering <color=#3366CC>Illinois</color> Democrats and labor unions nationwide; his support of the <color=#3366CC>gold</color>
<color=#3366CC>standard</color> and opposition to free silver alienated the <color=#3366CC>agrarian</color> wing of the Democrats. Critics complained that Cleveland
had little imagination and seemed overwhelmed by the nation's economic disasters—depressions and strikes—in his
second term. Many voters blamed the Democrats, opening the way for a Republican landslide in 1894 and for the
agrarian and free silver (silverite) seizure of the Democratic Party at the 1896 Democratic convention. By the end of his
second term, he was highly unpopular, even among Democrats.
After leaving the White House, Cleveland served as a trustee of <color=#3366CC>Princeton University</color>. He joined the American
Anti-Imperialist League in protest of the 1898 <color=#3366CC>Spanish–American War</color>. He died in 1908.
Early life
Childhood and family history
Stephen Grover Cleveland was born on March 18, 1837, in Caldwell, New Jersey, to Ann (née Neal) and Richard
Falley Cleveland. Cleveland's father, originally from <color=#3366CC>Connecticut</color>, was a Congregational and Presbyterian minister. His
mother was from <color=#3366CC>Baltimore</color> and was the daughter of a bookseller. On his father's side, Cleveland was descended from
English ancestors who first emigrated to <color=#3366CC>Massachusetts</color> from Ipswich, England, in 1635. On his mother's side,
Cleveland was descended from Anglo-Irish Protestants and German <color=#3366CC>Quakers</color>. Cleveland was distantly related to
General Moses Cleaveland, after whom the city of <color=#3366CC>Cleveland</color>, Ohio, was named.
Cleveland, the fifth of nine children, was named Stephen Grover in honor of the first pastor of the First Presbyterian
Church of Caldwell, where his father was pastor at the time. He became known as Grover in his adult life. In 1841, the
Cleveland family moved to Fayetteville, New York, where Grover spent much of his childhood. Neighbors later
described him as "full of fun and inclined to play pranks", and fond of outdoor sports.
In 1850, Cleveland's father Richard moved his family to Clinton, New York, accepting a job there as district secretary
